title: Open, save, exit
summary: Start nano on a file, read the shortcut bar, and leave with your changes saved (or not).

steps.title: Why learn a terminal editor at all
body: Sooner or later you are on a server over `ssh` with no VS Code, no mouse and a config file that needs one line changed. Every Linux box has at least one of **nano** or **vi**. Knowing both means you are never stuck.
**nano** is the easy one: what you type goes straight into the file, like Notepad. Start it with a file name:
```text
nano notes.txt              # opens notes.txt, or starts a new buffer that will be saved as notes.txt
nano /etc/hosts             # opening is fine; saving needs root (see lesson 3)
nano +25 app.conf           # open with the cursor on line 25
If the file does not exist, nano says `[ New File ]` at the bottom. Nothing is written to disk until you save.
> **Practise:** open **Labs → Vim & nano trainer** and run this lesson's challenges until the keys come without thinking.

steps.prompt: You run `nano todo.txt` in a folder where `todo.txt` does not exist, type two lines, then lose your connection. What is on disk?
options: Nothing: nano had not saved, so no file was created
steps.explain: Opening a new name only starts a buffer. The file appears when you write it out. (nano may leave an emergency `todo.txt.save` when it is killed by a hangup, which is a nice bonus, not a save.)

steps.title: The shortcut bar
body: The two bottom lines of nano list the most useful commands:
```text
^G Help      ^O Write Out ^W Where Is  ^K Cut       ^T Execute   ^C Location
^X Exit      ^R Read File ^\ Replace   ^U Paste     ^J Justify   ^_ Go To Line
- `^` means **Ctrl**: `^X` is Ctrl+X. You do not press Shift; `^x` and `^X` are the same key.
- `M-` means **Meta**, which is **Alt** on most keyboards (or press Esc, release, then the key): `M-U` is Alt+U (undo).
- `^G` opens the full help. You never have to memorise all of it: the bar is always there.

steps.prompt: In nano's shortcut bar, what does `^O Write Out` tell you to press?
steps.explain: `^` is the conventional notation for the Ctrl key. Write Out means save.

steps.prompt: Match each nano notation to the keys you press.
steps.explain: `M-` is Meta (Alt, or Esc then the key). `^_` really needs Shift because `_` is a shifted key.

steps.title: Saving and exiting
body: **Save**: `^O` (Write Out). nano shows `File Name to Write: notes.txt`; press **Enter** to accept the name (or edit it to save a copy elsewhere). Newer versions also save with `^S` without asking.
**Exit**: `^X`. If there are unsaved changes nano asks `Save modified buffer?`
```text
Y   save (then confirm the file name with Enter) and exit
N   throw the changes away and exit
^C  cancel: stay in the editor
So the classic "save and quit" is `^X`, `Y`, `Enter`.

steps.prompt: Put the keystrokes in order to save your changes and leave nano, starting while editing a modified file.
steps.explain: Exit asks to save; Y says yes; Enter confirms the file name.

steps.prompt: You opened a config, made a mess, and want to leave **without** saving anything. Which sequence?
steps.explain: N answers no to *Save modified buffer?*. `^C` at that prompt would cancel the exit and keep you in nano.

steps.prompt: Does the key sequence write the file to disk?

steps.title: Real keys: fix and write out
prompt: Now press the real keys. The trainer below runs a nano emulator in the page: it reacts to each key the way nano does.
Fix `Helo` to `Hello`, then save with **Write Out** (`^O`) and confirm the file name with Enter. The level is solved when the buffer is right and written to disk.
Browsers grab some Ctrl keys (Ctrl+W closes the tab). The trainer shows the other ways in, such as `Esc Esc O` for `^O`.
steps.explain: `^O` writes and keeps you in nano, which is what you want while you are still checking a config. `^X` is the one that leaves.
